A NAND gate with **both inputs tied together** acts as a **NOT** gate, so the
combination is OR followed by NOT - that is, **NOR**.
**Step 1 — write the OR output.**
X = **A + B** ✓
**Step 2 — feed X into both inputs of the NAND.**
Y = (X · X)′
= **X′** ✓
since X·X = X for any Boolean variable. A NAND with its inputs joined is simply an
**inverter**.
**Step 3 — substitute.**
Y = (A + B)′
= **A̅ · B̅** ✓
which is precisely the **NOR** function.
**Step 4 — check the truth table.**
A = 0, B = 0: OR gives 0, inverted → **1** ✓
A = 0, B = 1: OR gives 1 → **0** ✓
A = 1, B = 0: OR gives 1 → **0** ✓
A = 1, B = 1: OR gives 1 → **0** ✓
Output 1 only when **both** inputs are 0 - the NOR table exactly ✓
**Why a tied-input NAND inverts.** NAND gives 0 only when both inputs are 1 ✓ Tie them
together and the gate sees either 0,0 → output **1**, or 1,1 → output **0**. That is
inversion.
**The same trick with NOR.** A NOR gate with its inputs joined is **also** an
inverter ✓ which is why both NAND and NOR are called **universal gates**: any logic
function whatever can be built from copies of either one alone.
**Why universality matters.** A chip foundry need master only **one** gate type ✓
Standard logic families are built almost entirely from NAND or NOR, with AND, OR and
NOT assembled from them.
**How to build the others from NAND.**
NOT: tie the inputs ✓
AND: NAND followed by NOT ✓
OR: invert both inputs, then NAND - by De Morgan's law ✓
**De Morgan's laws, which underlie all this.**
(A + B)′ = **A̅ · B̅** ✓
(A · B)′ = **A̅ + B̅** ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **AND** ✗ would need the OR replaced by an AND. **NAND** ✗
is the second gate alone. **NOT** ✗ ignores the OR stage ✓
∴ NOR gate.

Two NOR gates used as **inverters** feeding a third NOR gives an **AND**.
**Step 1 — read the first stage.** A is fed to a NOR gate with **both inputs joined**,
so the output is
(A + A)′ = **A̅** ✓
and likewise the second gate gives **B̅** ✓ Each acts as an inverter.
**Step 2 — read the final stage.** The two inverted signals go into a third NOR:
Y = (A̅ + B̅)′ ✓
**Step 3 — apply De Morgan's law.**
(A̅ + B̅)′ = **A · B** ✓
the **AND** function.
**Step 4 — verify with the truth table.**
A = 0, B = 0: A̅ = 1, B̅ = 1, NOR(1,1) = **0** ✓
A = 0, B = 1: 1, 0 → NOR = **0** ✓
A = 1, B = 0: 0, 1 → NOR = **0** ✓
A = 1, B = 1: 0, 0 → NOR = **1** ✓
Output 1 only when **both** inputs are 1 - the AND table ✓
**Why a NOR with tied inputs inverts.** NOR outputs 1 only when both inputs are 0 ✓
With the inputs joined: 0,0 → **1**; 1,1 → **0**. That is a NOT gate.
**The De Morgan insight.** "**NOT both zero**" is the same as "**at least one is
one**", and inverting the inputs of a NOR turns it into an AND ✓ Every such conversion
is an application of these two laws.
**Why NOR is universal.** Any logic function can be built from NOR gates alone ✓
NOT: tie the inputs ✓
OR: NOR followed by a NOR-inverter ✓
AND: invert both inputs, then NOR ✓ which is exactly this circuit
**Where NOR-only logic was used.** The **Apollo Guidance Computer** was built entirely
from about 5600 three-input NOR gates ✓ a striking demonstration of universality.
**How to recognise such circuits quickly.** Look for NOR or NAND gates with **joined
inputs** - they are inverters ✓ Then apply De Morgan to the final stage.
**Reading the distractors.** **NOR** ✗ would be the output if A and B went **directly**
into the third gate. **OR** ✗ needs one further inversion, and **NAND** ✗ is the
complement of the answer ✓
∴ AND-Gate.

Convert α to β with **β = α/(1 − α)**.
**Step 1 — recall the relation.**
α = I_C/I_E and β = I_C/I_B ✓
and since I_E = I_B + I_C,
**β = α/(1 − α)** ✓
**Step 2 — substitute.**
β = 0·98/(1 − 0·98)
= 0·98/0·02 ✓
**Step 3 — evaluate.**
= **49** ✓
**What the numbers mean.** 98% of the emitter current reaches the collector, and only
**2%** is lost to recombination in the base ✓ The collector current is therefore 49
times the base current.
**How sensitive β is to α.** Extremely ✓
α = 0·98 → β = **49**
α = 0·99 → β = **99**
α = 0·995 → β = **199**
A half-per-cent improvement in base transport **doubles** the gain - which is why
transistors of the same type can have β differing by a factor of three, and why good
amplifier designs use **negative feedback** so the gain depends on resistors rather
than on β.
**The inverse relation.**
α = β/(1 + β) ✓
Here 49/50 = **0·98** ✓ confirming the answer.
**Why α is always just below 1.** Some recombination in the base is unavoidable ✓ α = 1
would mean a perfect transistor with infinite β.
**How the design maximises α.** A **thin**, **lightly doped** base ✓ Thin so carriers
cross before recombining; lightly doped so there are few carriers of the opposite type
to recombine with.
**A worked check.** With I_B = 1 mA:
I_C = β I_B = **49 mA**
I_E = I_B + I_C = **50 mA**
α = 49/50 = **0·98** ✓ exactly as given.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·49** ✗ and **4·9** ✗ are α/2 and α x 5, matching no
relation. **5** ✗ would correspond to α = 0·833 ✓ Checking with α = β/(1 + β) tests any
candidate in one line.
∴ 49.

The **input** characteristic plots the input current against the input voltage, with
the **output** voltage held fixed.
**Step 1 — identify the input and output of CE mode.** In **common emitter**:
input: the **base-emitter** circuit, with current **I_B** and voltage **V_BE** ✓
output: the **collector-emitter** circuit, with **I_C** and **V_CE** ✓
**Step 2 — state what an input characteristic is.** A plot of the **input current**
against the **input voltage**, at a **constant output voltage** ✓ So
**I_B against V_BE at constant V_CE** ✓
**What the curve looks like.** Exactly like a **forward-biased diode** characteristic ✓
negligible current until V_BE reaches about **0·7 V** for silicon, then a steep
exponential rise. That is no accident - the base-emitter junction **is** a
forward-biased diode.
**Why V_CE must be held constant.** Changing it slightly alters the effective base
width - the **Early effect** - and shifts the curve ✓ A family of input curves at
different V_CE lies very close together, which is why the input characteristic is often
drawn as a single line.
**What is read from it.** The **input resistance**
r_i = ΔV_BE/ΔI_B at constant V_CE ✓
typically a few **hundred ohms to a few kilohms** - low, which is characteristic of a
forward-biased junction.
**The companion curve.** The **output** characteristic plots **I_C against V_CE at
constant I_B** ✓ It shows a steep rise through the saturation region and then a nearly
flat active region, from which the output resistance and the current gain β are read.
**Why the pair is needed.** Together they define the transistor's behaviour completely
and allow the **load line** to be drawn, fixing the operating point ✓
**Why the input and output cannot be mixed.** Plotting I_B against V_CE ✗ gives almost
a flat line, since the base current barely depends on the collector voltage ✓ and
plotting I_B against I_C merely reproduces β.
**Reading the distractors.** Each alternative swaps one variable ✓ The rule is simple:
**input current vs input voltage**, with the **other side's voltage** held constant.
∴ I_B against V_BE at constant V_CE.

A **Zener diode** holds a steady voltage across itself in reverse breakdown, which is
exactly what a regulator needs.
**Step 1 — recall the Zener's characteristic.** Operated in **reverse** bias, it conducts
negligibly until the **breakdown voltage** V_Z is reached ✓ Beyond that the current
rises almost vertically while the **voltage stays essentially constant**.
**Step 2 — see why that regulates.** Any attempt to raise the voltage across the diode
causes a large increase in current through the series resistor, dropping the surplus ✓
The load therefore sees a fixed **V_Z** whatever the supply does within limits.
**Step 3 — describe the circuit.** A series resistor R takes up the difference between
the unregulated supply and V_Z, and the Zener sits in **parallel** with the load ✓
R = (V_in − V_Z)/(I_Z + I_L)
**Why the breakdown is not destructive.** Unlike an ordinary diode, a Zener is designed
for it ✓ Provided the **power** V_Z I_Z stays within its rating, the breakdown is
entirely reversible and may be repeated indefinitely.
**The two mechanisms.**
**Zener breakdown** proper, below about 5 V - quantum **tunnelling** across a heavily
doped, very narrow junction ✓
**avalanche breakdown**, above about 6 V - carriers accelerated enough to ionise
others ✓
Both give the same sharp characteristic, and commercial "Zener" diodes are available
from about 2·4 V to 200 V.
**Why the other devices do not regulate.**
**photodiode** ✗ - a light **detector**, its reverse current proportional to
illumination; used in light meters and optical receivers
**laser diode** ✗ - emits coherent light; used in CD players and fibre
communications ✓
**solar cell** ✗ - a photovoltaic **source**, converting light to electrical power
Each is a p-n device, but none holds a constant voltage.
**The limitation of a simple Zener regulator.** It wastes power in the series resistor
and handles only modest currents ✓ For larger loads it serves as the **reference** for
an integrated regulator or a transistor pass element.
∴ Zener diode.

The emitter must **supply** the carriers, so it is **heavily doped**; it is of
**moderate size**, between the thin base and the large collector.
**Step 1 — see what the emitter does.** It **injects** charge carriers into the base ✓
To supply them in quantity it must have a high concentration of majority carriers -
hence **heavy doping**.
**Step 2 — compare the three regions.**
**emitter**: **moderate** size, **heavily** doped ✓ - supplies the carriers
**base**: **very thin**, **lightly** doped ✓ - so that almost all carriers cross without
recombining
**collector**: **largest**, **moderately** doped ✓ - to collect the carriers and
dissipate the heat
**Step 3 — conclude.** The emitter is **moderate in size and heavily doped** ✓
**Why the base must be thin and lightly doped.** So that **95 to 99%** of the injected
carriers reach the collector ✓ A thick or heavily doped base would lose most of them to
recombination, destroying the current gain:
β = I_C/I_B, which depends entirely on how few are lost ✓
**Why the collector is the largest.** Carriers arriving there have been accelerated
across a **reverse-biased** junction, and the power dissipated appears as heat ✓ A large
collector region, usually bonded to the metal case or a heat sink, spreads and removes
it.
**Why the transistor is not symmetric.** Emitter and collector differ in both **size**
and **doping**, so swapping them gives the poor **reverse-active** mode with a current
gain of perhaps 2 instead of 100 ✓ The circuit symbol's arrow marks the emitter for
exactly this reason.
**A typical set of doping levels.**
emitter: **10²⁵ m⁻³**
base: **10²³ m⁻³** ✓
collector: **10²¹ m⁻³**
a hundredfold step down at each stage.
**The base thickness.** About **1 µm** or less in a modern device ✓ far shorter than
the carriers' diffusion length, which is what guarantees they cross.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Large and lightly doped**" ✗ describes neither region
correctly. "**Thin and heavily doped**" ✗ confuses the emitter's doping with the base's
size. "**Large and moderately doped**" ✗ describes the **collector** ✓
∴ moderate size and heavily doped.

n-type needs a **pentavalent** dopant and p-type a **trivalent** one - so the pair must
be phosphorus and indium.
**Step 1 — classify the four elements named.**
**arsenic** - group 15, **pentavalent** → n-type ✓
**phosphorus** - group 15, **pentavalent** → n-type ✓
**indium** - group 13, **trivalent** → p-type ✓
**aluminium** - group 13, **trivalent** → p-type ✓
**boron** - group 13, **trivalent** → p-type ✓
**Step 2 — test each option.**
**arsenic and phosphorus** ✗ - both pentavalent, so **both** would give n-type
**indium and aluminium** ✗ - both trivalent, so **both** would give p-type
**phosphorus and indium** ✓ - pentavalent then trivalent, giving **n-type then
p-type** - exactly as asked
**aluminium and boron** ✗ - both trivalent again
**Step 3 — conclude.** Only one option pairs a donor with an acceptor **in that
order** ✓
**Why a pentavalent atom gives n-type.** It has **one electron too many** for the four
covalent bonds of silicon ✓ That spare electron is bound by only about **0·05 eV**, so
room temperature frees it at once - a mobile **negative** carrier, hence "n".
**Why a trivalent atom gives p-type.** It has **one too few**, leaving a **hole** ✓ which
accepts an electron from a neighbouring bond and migrates as a mobile **positive**
carrier.
**The mnemonic, and its trap.** **P**entavalent gives **n**-type; **tri**valent gives
**p**-type ✓ The letters are deliberately crossed, so count the **valence electrons**
rather than trusting the initials.
**The order matters.** The question asks for n-type **and** p-type "respectively", so
the donor must be named **first** ✓ Reversing them would be wrong even with the right
two elements.
**Typical doping levels.** About **one part in 10⁶ to 10⁸** ✓ enough to multiply the
conductivity a thousandfold while leaving the crystal structure untouched.
**Why both materials stay neutral.** Each dopant atom is neutral when added ✓ Once it
donates or accepts an electron it becomes a **fixed ion**, exactly balanced by the
mobile carrier it released.
∴ Phosphorous and Indium respectively.
